title: Week 123 · Lesson 147: Advance Care Planning, Serious-Illness Communication, Palliative Care & Hospice — FNP-Level Goal-Concordant Care
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 123 — Lesson 147: Advance Care Planning, Serious-Illness Communication, Palliative Care & Hospice

FNP-level goal: Translate a patient's values into medically informed, legally appropriate, and operational care plans; communicate prognosis with honesty and uncertainty; distinguish advance directives, surrogate authority, portable medical orders, code status, palliative care, and hospice; and coordinate symptom relief and emergency planning without abandoning treatable suffering.

Learning Objectives

  • Initiate advance care planning before crisis and update it after meaningful health or life changes.
  • Distinguish a living will, health-care proxy, surrogate, DNR/DNI, and POLST/MOLST or other portable medical orders.
  • Assess decision-specific capacity and guide surrogates using substituted judgment and best-interest standards.
  • Use serious-illness communication to connect prognosis, tradeoffs, and recommendations with what matters most.
  • Differentiate palliative care from hospice and coordinate symptom, medication, caregiver, spiritual, and emergency care.

Part 1 — Advance Care Planning Is a Process

Advance care planning prepares for future medical decisions if a person becomes seriously ill or cannot communicate. The central intervention is a continuing conversation about values, acceptable function, fears, tradeoffs, and trusted decision-makers. A signed form without understanding or availability may fail during crisis.

Planning is appropriate for all adults, not only people who are old or dying. Review it after a new serious diagnosis, hospitalization, functional decline, change in relationship, move across state lines, death of a proxy, or change in goals. The best plan evolves with the person.

Part 2 — Start With Values Before Procedures

Questions about CPR, ventilation, feeding tubes, dialysis, or hospitalization make sense only in a clinical context. First ask what makes life meaningful, what abilities are essential, what outcomes would be unacceptable, what the patient fears, and how much burden they would accept for a chance of recovery.

Preferences may depend on reversibility and time. A patient may accept short-term ventilation for pneumonia with a good chance of recovery but decline prolonged support after devastating neurologic injury. Document the condition and purpose, not only yes or no.

Part 3 — Living Will

A living will is an advance directive that describes treatment preferences for circumstances in which the patient cannot make or communicate decisions. State forms and legal requirements vary. General phrases such as no heroic measures may be difficult to interpret without discussion.

Encourage condition-specific guidance: whether the person prioritizes longevity, cognition, communication, comfort, home, or a time-limited trial. Give copies to the proxy, health system, and relevant care settings and ensure the current version replaces outdated copies.

Part 4 — Health-Care Power of Attorney and Proxy

A durable power of attorney for health care names an agent, proxy, or representative to make health decisions when the patient lacks capacity under applicable law. Financial power of attorney is a different role and does not automatically confer health-care authority.

Select someone willing to honor the patient's values, ask questions, manage conflict, and be available. An ideal proxy is not necessarily the closest relative. Discuss alternate agents and state restrictions on who may serve.

Part 5 — Surrogates Without a Named Proxy

When no valid proxy is named and the patient lacks capacity, state law commonly defines a surrogate hierarchy or process. An unmarried partner, close friend, or distant family member may or may not have authority depending on jurisdiction.

Confirm legal authority rather than allowing the loudest relative to decide. When no suitable surrogate exists or conflict persists, involve ethics, social work, legal counsel, guardianship or court pathways as appropriate, while urgent treatment follows emergency standards and known wishes.

Part 6 — Capacity Is Decision Specific and Can Fluctuate

Connect Lessons 141 and 146: capacity requires the ability to understand relevant information, appreciate how it applies, reason about options, and communicate a choice. Diagnosis, age, family disagreement, or a low screening score does not automatically remove it.

Treat delirium, pain, hypoxia, medication toxicity, language, hearing, and timing barriers. A patient may have capacity to select a proxy but not to weigh a complex high-risk procedure. Document the specific decision and supporting abilities.

Part 7 — Substituted Judgment and Best Interest

A surrogate should first represent what the patient would choose based on prior statements, values, and way of life—substituted judgment. If those preferences are unknown, use the patient's best interest by weighing benefits, burdens, suffering, dignity, and medical options.

The surrogate's personal preference is not the standard. Ask, What would the patient say if they could understand this situation? Family conflict often softens when attention returns to the patient's voice.

Part 8 — POLST, MOLST, POST, and Portable Medical Orders

POLST and related state programs convert current goals of a seriously ill or advanced-frailty patient into portable medical orders that clinicians and emergency personnel can act on. They are not substitutes for an advance directive and generally are not intended for healthy adults.

Forms, names, authorized signers, sections, registries, and revocation rules vary by state. Complete them after an informed conversation, not as routine admission paperwork. Review after transfer, substantial condition change, or changed goals, and keep the form accessible.

Part 9 — DNR Means No CPR After Arrest

A do-not-resuscitate order applies when the patient has no pulse and is not breathing. It does not mean no antibiotics, no oxygen, no pain treatment, no hospitalization, or no treatment before arrest. A do-not-intubate order addresses ventilation and should be clarified separately.

Explain likely CPR outcomes in the patient's clinical context rather than asking, Do you want us to do everything? A recommendation may be appropriate when CPR cannot achieve the patient's goals, but the conversation must remain respectful and legally sound.

Part 10 — Avoid the False Choice of Everything or Nothing

Care always continues. The question is which treatments provide benefit consistent with the goal. A comfort-focused patient may still receive a fracture repair, antibiotics for distressing infection, diuresis for dyspnea, transfusion, or hospitalization when those interventions improve comfort and are desired.

Likewise, choosing disease treatment does not exclude symptom control. Present options as goal-linked plans rather than abandonment versus maximal technology.

Part 11 — Palliative Care

Palliative care is specialized interdisciplinary care for serious illness focused on symptoms, communication, psychosocial and spiritual needs, caregiver support, and care coordination. It can begin at any age or disease stage and can accompany disease-directed or potentially curative treatment.

Refer based on need, not a precise prognosis: complex pain or dyspnea, repeated hospitalization, difficult decisions, distress, caregiver overload, treatment conflict, or declining function. Primary palliative skills belong in FNP practice, while specialty teams add expertise for complexity.

Part 12 — Hospice

Hospice is a model and benefit for terminal illness when care goals focus on comfort rather than cure of the terminal condition. Under the Medicare benefit, the attending physician if present and the hospice physician certify a prognosis of six months or less if the illness follows its normal course; ongoing eligibility can be recertified.

Hospice is not limited to cancer and is not a promise that death will occur on an exact date. Eligibility, election, covered services, setting, certification roles, and payment rules require current CMS and local hospice guidance. Patients can ask questions, compare agencies, and revoke an election under applicable rules.

Part 13 — Do Not Wait for the Final Days

Late referrals deprive patients and caregivers of symptom expertise, equipment, teaching, respite, and crisis planning. Consider hospice when disease is progressive, function and intake decline, hospitalizations recur, and burdensome treatment no longer supports the patient's goals.

Use the surprise question only as a prompt, not an eligibility test. A clinician's uncertainty should lead to discussion and hospice evaluation rather than silence.

Part 14 — Prognosis Is a Range, Not a Date

Explain what is known, what is uncertain, and the most likely trajectory. Offer ranges such as days to weeks, weeks to months, or months to years when supported. Describe function, cognition, intake, and likely complications as well as survival.

Ask permission: Would it be okay if I shared what I expect? Use best-case, worst-case, and most-likely scenarios when uncertainty is substantial. Revisit predictions as the illness changes.

Part 15 — Serious-Illness Communication

Prepare a quiet setting, include the chosen people, confirm decision-making capacity, and use a professional interpreter. Ask what the patient understands and how much detail they want. Give a concise warning statement before difficult information and pause for emotion.

Name and validate emotion before delivering more data: This is a lot to take in. Then explore values, summarize, and make a recommendation tied to the goal. Ask the patient to teach back the plan and document unresolved questions.

Part 16 — Make a Goal-Concordant Recommendation

Do not leave a frightened family with a menu of procedures and no guidance. State the medical judgment: Given that being able to communicate at home matters most, and this treatment is unlikely to restore that ability, I recommend a comfort-focused plan.

Recommendations must reflect the patient's values, not clinician bias about age or disability. Discuss uncertainty and alternatives, and allow time when the situation permits.

Part 17 — Time-Limited Trials

When outcome is uncertain, a time-limited trial can align treatment with goals. Define the intervention, duration, measurable signs of improvement, burdens, who will reassess, and what happens if the target is not met.

A trial without a stopping rule becomes indefinite treatment. Examples include ventilation, dialysis, artificial nutrition, rehabilitation, or hospitalization. Ensure the surrogate understands that stopping an ineffective trial is completion of the agreed plan, not abandonment.

Part 18 — Symptom Assessment Is Multidimensional

Assess pain, dyspnea, nausea, constipation, fatigue, anxiety, depression, insomnia, delirium, secretions, wounds, appetite, and spiritual or existential distress. Ask how symptoms affect function and family. Use patient report when possible and validated behavioral tools when communication is impaired.

Look for reversible causes consistent with goals: urinary retention, fecal impaction, medication toxicity, hypoxia, fracture, infection, heart failure, or uncontrolled pain. Comfort care does not mean ignoring treatable suffering.

Part 19 — Pain

Clarify nociceptive, neuropathic, inflammatory, ischemic, visceral, and total-pain contributors. Combine nonpharmacologic support with medicines selected for kidney, liver, bleeding, delirium, and fall risk. Establish a rescue and constipation plan when opioids are used.

Opioids may be appropriate for serious-illness pain when benefits outweigh risks. Titrate to comfort and function, monitor sedation and breathing, and educate caregivers. Fear of addiction should not cause untreated terminal suffering, while comfort goals do not justify careless dosing.

Part 20 — Dyspnea

Assess airway, oxygenation, infection, edema, anemia, effusion, embolism, anxiety, and mechanical contributors according to goals. Upright position, airflow from a fan, calm coaching, treatment of bronchospasm or congestion, and oxygen for hypoxemia may help.

Systemic opioids can reduce refractory dyspnea in selected serious-illness patients under an individualized plan. Start cautiously, reassess relief and adverse effects, and coordinate specialty support for complex patients. Severe new dyspnea may still require emergency evaluation when consistent with goals.

Part 21 — Nausea, Constipation, and Delirium

Match antiemetic strategy to likely mechanism and medication burden. Prevent opioid constipation proactively unless diarrhea or obstruction changes the plan. Assess impaction, obstruction, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and urinary retention.

For delirium, treat reversible causes that fit goals, restore hearing and vision, reduce unnecessary medicines, orient gently, and support sleep. Sedating medication may be considered for severe distress or danger after assessment; routine sedation is not a substitute for care.

Part 22 — Deprescribing in Serious Illness

Review each medicine for current goal, time to benefit, withdrawal risk, symptom value, burden, route, and monitoring. Long-horizon preventive treatment may no longer help, while analgesics, diuretics, inhalers, anticonvulsants, or antidepressants may remain essential.

Taper dependence-producing medicines when appropriate and simplify schedules. Explain that deprescribing removes treatments that no longer serve the plan; it does not mean the person no longer matters.

Part 23 — Nutrition and Hydration

Loss of appetite and intake may be part of advanced illness. Offer preferred foods, mouth care, small portions, and assistance without forcing. Artificial nutrition and hydration have condition-specific benefits and burdens and should be discussed in relation to reversibility, aspiration, fluid overload, discomfort, prognosis, and values.

A feeding tube does not automatically prevent aspiration or restore function in advanced dementia. Support careful hand feeding and comfort when aligned with goals. Avoid framing family decisions as feeding versus starving.

Part 24 — Spiritual, Cultural, and Family Context

Ask what gives strength, whether faith or cultural practices affect decisions, and whom the patient wants involved. Do not assign beliefs based on ethnicity or religion. Offer chaplaincy or community spiritual support with permission.

Family members may disagree because they love the patient, understand prognosis differently, feel guilt, or carry prior conflict. Use consistent information, identify the authorized decision-maker, and return to the patient's values. Ethics or mediation support may help.

Part 25 — Caregiver Assessment

Ask about sleep, physical ability, depression, grief, finances, medication administration, emergency confidence, work, other dependents, and respite. A plan that requires care the family cannot provide is not safe.

Teach what changes to expect, whom to call day and night, medication use, safe transfers, mouth and skin care, and what to do during a crisis. Hospice and palliative teams can support caregivers, but the FNP should verify that contacts and supplies are actually available.

Part 26 — Emergency Planning

Specify whether the patient wants hospitalization for reversible problems, where care should occur, which symptoms prompt a call, who has the portable orders, and how EMS can access them. Ensure current forms and proxy contact information travel across home, facility, dialysis, clinic, and hospital.

A DNR hidden in an inaccessible chart may not guide EMS. A crisis plan should be visible without compromising privacy and should match local law and emergency systems.

Part 27 — When Goals Change

A capable patient can revise preferences. Review orders after a major diagnosis, hospitalization, treatment result, functional change, transfer, or new understanding. Confirm that older conflicting forms are removed and the updated plan reaches all care settings.

A change in mind is not failure. It may reflect new experience, priorities, prognosis, or acceptable burden. Document the conversation and capacity at the time.

Part 28 — Conflict and Potentially Nonbeneficial Treatment

When requested treatment is unlikely to achieve its physiologic purpose or the patient's goals, clarify misunderstandings, emotions, cultural needs, and prior promises. Provide a clear recommendation and seek palliative, ethics, specialty, or legal consultation according to policy.

Do not label families difficult or act unilaterally outside law and policy. Continue symptom relief and communication during conflict. Transfer processes may be required when clinicians or institutions cannot provide requested care.

Part 29 — FNP Scope and Team Roles

FNP roles include advance care planning, capacity screening, primary symptom management, medication review, caregiver support, documentation, referral, and care coordination. Authority to sign portable orders, certify hospice eligibility, prescribe controlled substances, or act as an attending varies by state, payer, and organization.

Collaborate with physicians, palliative specialists, hospice, nurses, social workers, pharmacists, chaplains, therapists, legal or ethics teams, and community supports. Verify scope rather than assuming that one rule applies everywhere.

Part 30 — Documentation

Record participants, capacity, interpreter, patient understanding, values, prognosis discussed, treatments considered, benefits and burdens, recommendation, decisions, surrogate authority, forms completed, copies distributed, follow-up, and unresolved conflict.

A checkbox saying goals discussed is insufficient. The next clinician should understand what matters, what was decided, under which conditions, and whom to call.

Part 31 — Red Flags and Immediate Care

Advance plans do not override a currently capable patient's request or excuse neglect of acute suffering. Emergency evaluation may be needed for severe uncontrolled symptoms, airway compromise, major hemorrhage, fracture, acute stroke, unsafe caregiver situation, medication error, or inability to deliver the agreed plan, depending on goals and orders.

If documents conflict, capacity is uncertain, or the surrogate cannot be reached during an emergency, follow applicable law, institutional policy, and emergency standards while urgently clarifying the patient's known wishes.

Clinical Case 1 — DNR Is Not Do Not Treat

An 84-year-old with a DNR develops painful urinary retention and delirium. A staff member suggests comfort only means no evaluation. The FNP clarifies that DNR applies to CPR after arrest, treats retention and pain, evaluates reversible delirium causes, and confirms whether hospitalization fits the broader goals.

Clinical Case 2 — A Time-Limited Trial

A patient with advanced COPD values returning home but has potentially reversible pneumonia and uncertain recovery. After discussing best, worst, and most-likely outcomes, the patient chooses a short trial of noninvasive support with defined respiratory, cognitive, and mobility targets and a transition to comfort-focused care if those targets are not met.

Clinical Case 3 — Hospice Is Not Giving Up

A 79-year-old with progressive metastatic disease, recurrent admissions, declining intake, and a goal to remain home believes hospice means no medication and immediate death. The FNP explains the benefit, eligibility evaluation, continued symptom treatment, team support, recertification if eligibility persists, and the patient's right to reconsider, then arranges an informational hospice visit.

FNP High-Yield Framework: VALUES

  1. V — Verify voice: capacity, proxy, surrogate authority, interpreter, participants.
  2. A — Ask what matters: function, relationships, fears, unacceptable outcomes, place of care.
  3. L — Lay out prognosis: understanding, uncertainty, best, worst, and most likely.
  4. U — Unite goals and treatments: benefit, burden, recommendation, time-limited trial.
  5. E — Execute the plan: directive, POLST/MOLST, code status, symptom and emergency orders.
  6. S — Share and sustain: copies, caregiver teaching, team referral, review after change.

Take-Home Summary

Goal-concordant care requires more than a form. FNP-level practice assesses capacity, identifies the patient's values and authorized voice, communicates prognosis honestly, recommends treatments that serve the goal, and makes the plan available across settings. Palliative care can accompany disease treatment; hospice is a specific terminal-illness model and benefit; and DNR addresses CPR rather than all care.

Educational note: Apply current NIA advance-care-planning, CMS and Medicare hospice, National POLST, state surrogate and portable-order law, controlled-substance, payer, scope, and institutional guidance. Severe uncontrolled symptoms, acute injury, unsafe care, conflicting orders, or uncertain authority requires prompt clinical, palliative, ethics, legal, or emergency support consistent with the patient's known goals.
